opus-5.5.text:
I think what's interesting about it is that it was written by students, for students, and it was very honest. It wasn't an official document. It basically said: the system you're entering may not be designed to help you learn the way you actually want to learn, so you need to take responsibility for your own education.

When I was at Jiao Tong, a lot of people passed it around. The message that stuck with people was roughly: don't assume high grades equal real understanding. Many courses were taught in a way that rewarded memorizing for exams, and the guide was frank about that. It encouraged you to figure out what you care about, find good resources yourself, read textbooks and open courses from other places, and not treat the GPA game as the whole point of university.

Looking back, that mindset matters a lot, especially for research. In research nobody hands you a syllabus. You have to decide what problem is worth working on, teach yourself whatever you're missing, and be comfortable when the "standard path" isn't the right one. In a way, the guide was an early lesson in that kind of independence.

It also captured a bit of that era's spirit. The internet was opening up, and students suddenly realized they could access MIT lectures or classic textbooks directly. There was a sense of: the walls of the classroom aren't the boundary anymore. I think that feeling of "you can go learn from the best in the world on your own" shaped a lot of people of my generation, including those of us who ended up in AI.

Of course, it was a bit rebellious and one-sided in places. But I think its core idea, that your education is ultimately your own responsibility, still holds up really well.

r002.rationale: It describes independence in research and deciding what problem to work on, but does not identify exploring the unknown as research’s purpose.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, the Survival Guide — that thing was honestly formative for me. I came into Shanghai Jiao Tong as a freshman not really knowing anything, and someone handed me this document, this huge collection of advice written by upperclassmen, and it felt like a kind of secret knowledge being passed down.

What I found interesting about it, looking back, is that it wasn't just "here's how to pick courses" or "here's which canteen has the best food." It was really about how to think about your own time at university. There was this underlying message that the curriculum is not the point — the curriculum is a floor, not a ceiling — and that you have to take ownership of your own education. Go read the original papers, go talk to professors, go find the people who are actually doing interesting things on campus. That was a pretty radical framing for an eighteen-year-old who had spent the last several years optimizing for gaokao.

The other thing I appreciated was that it was written by students, for students, with no official stamp on it. It was honest in a way an official handbook could never be. It told you which things were worth your energy and which were just bureaucratic noise. And it was self-perpetuating — people kept editing it and adding to it, so it was this living document shaped by many generations of students.

I think a lot of my later attitude toward research came from that mindset. The idea that you shouldn't wait for someone to tell you what's important, that you should go explore the boundaries yourself — that started there for me, long before I got to grad school or started working on computer vision.

r002.rationale: It connects research with exploring boundaries, but does not clearly identify exploring the unknown as the purpose of research.

astra-6.text: What I find interesting is the idea of a “survival guide” written by students for other students. The official materials can tell you what courses to take and what requirements to fulfill, but they don’t necessarily help you think through what you want from those years. Even the title acknowledges that students may feel lost, and that’s something worth talking about openly. I’d approach a guide like that as a collection of perspectives—something to question and learn from as you find your own path.

r002.rationale: The response describes finding one’s own path through the guide, but does not identify exploring the unknown as the purpose of research.

sol-6.1.text: What I find interesting is the idea of students sharing the things they wish someone had told them earlier. An official handbook can explain the rules, but a survival guide can address a different question: what is it actually like to be a student here? How do you find your interests, ask for help, and decide what deserves your time? That kind of peer-to-peer knowledge can be really valuable, especially when you’re just starting out.
